article.title: California’s Climate Law Still Matters Globally
article.author: Joe Mathews
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Why should you still care about AB 32, two decades after Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger signed it into law? Not just because the “California Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006” remains in effect, and enjoys support of 75% of state residents, according to a 2026 poll by the Public Policy Institute of California. Nor because AB 32 is the foundation for California’s climate regulation regime has reduced per-capita greenhouse gas emissions by 29%. Nor because it is the closest thing the U.S. has to a national climate law, as the Trump administration boosts fossil fuels and cancels regulations. You should care about AB 32 because no law in modern world history better demonstrates what we can do for the planet—and better exposes our shortcomings. AB 32 was the first law anywhere to set legally enforceable, economy-wide standards for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. For climate, it’s like the Magna Carta and Declaration of Independence, rolled into one. Related: The Next Big Shift in California’s Climate Change Movement Just as Britain’s 1215 Magna Carta claimed that no king or queen was above the rule of law, AB 32 established the principle that no polluter or planetary system on Earth was beyond the reach of law—even local, California-only law. Just as the Declaration of Independence defied the authority the British monarchy, AB 32 defied the George W. Bush administration, which had blocked climate action and boosted fossil fuel subsidies. As the world’s nations walked away from the 1998 Kyoto Protocol , it provided an example of climate policy leadership for provincial and local governments worldwide. AB 32-style laws were adopted by Hawaiʻi, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Connecticut, and regulations from the law have been adopted in dozens of states. But it may be most necessary today as inspiration. In 2026, it can feel like all is lost. Global warming is accelerating . Glacial ice and ocean currents are collapsing. Yet many governments are unresponsive. But in 2006, everything felt lost in California. Climate change was accelerating then , too. The Golden State was fighting another warmongering federal government hostile to the environment. The state budget was a mess, and a disastrous special election in 2005 fueled bitter political divides. This toxic environment nonetheless produced a breakthrough in AB 32. The story of how that positive change happened is worth remembering. Today, we tell ourselves that politics is blood sport, and there is no room for bipartisanship and friendship. But AB 32 was built on friendship and compromise between political antagonists, the Democratic Assembly Speaker Fabian Núñez and Schwarzenegger, the Republican governor. It was also created by politically diverse teams. A leading organization behind the bill, E2, was an alliance of environmentalists and entrepreneurs. And Schwarzenegger’s administration, a mix of Democrats and Republicans, was the closest thing in America’s modern history to a coalition government. Despite Republican allies’ warnings against “employing enemies,” Schwarzenegger relied heavily on advisors who had worked for Gov. Gray Davis, whom he had replaced in the 2003 recall. Núñez and Schwarzenegger, who both lacked scientific training and long track records on the environment, warmly welcomed outsiders and opponents into their conference rooms. Ideas emerged from unusual places. A former America’s Cup sailboat captain came up a precursor bill regulating car exhaust. A crucial rule was drafted in a Buenos Aires bar. The original author of AB 32, Fran Pavley, was a career middle-school teacher, elected to the Assembly almost by accident. She made a point of meeting with every single member of the legislature as she shaped her bill. Instead of despairing during crisis, AB 32’s creators leaned into it. State government had created California’s 2000-2001 electricity crisis and its manipulated markets, rolling blackouts, and surging bills. But, as former Davis aide Kurt Schuparra describes in his book, How the California Electricity Crisis Generated a Green Wave , two administrations’ creative response to the crisis advanced renewable energy and opened the door for AB 32. And when opposition grew, California’s leaders did not narrow their vision, as commonly happens with controversial legislation. They raised the stakes, with Schwarzenegger recruiting international supporters like British Prime Minister Tony Blair and oil giant BP CEO Lord John Browne to create global pressure to pass the bill. AB 32’s backers weren’t sure it would pass until the very end of the legislative session. The federal government said it was illegal, a preemption of U.S. law. Schwarzenegger’s own party sought to sabotage it, and the governor considered vetoing it. The historic victory happened anyway. AB 32 required California to reduce its statewide greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels by 2020. It was a massive legal risk, and a demand that tomorrow’s needs take precedence over present-day politics. In several ways, AB 32 delivered on its promise. The state hit its 2020 target for greenhouse gas reductions in 2016 . AB 32 sparked new businesses like electric cars, produced more than 550,000 clean energy jobs, and generated $36 billion through its cap-and-trade program. according to Next 10 , which tracks California’s climate policy. Globally, California has built partnerships with dozens of nations, and shared technology and regulations with provinces and cities, including several in China . Yet, for all its success, AB 32 is also a human story of mistakes and limitations. Political momentum for countering climate change has slowed, even in California, where fights about the balance between markets and direct regulation in reducing emissions have never ended. The state’s 2030 targets for greenhouse gas reductions are unlikely to be met. And global climate change is worsening as earthlings decarbonize too slowly. But for all the follow-up legislation and regulation the law has inspired, as well as its two renewals (most recently last year, through 2045), California has failed to build the technological, political, and legal infrastructure needed to win the climate fight. What might that infrastructure look like? The most compelling answer I can find comes from UC San Diego climate policy scholar David Victor, and Columbia Law School’s Charles Sabel, who argued in a 2022 book that our current system no longer works for a world of such uncertainty. They urge us to embrace “experimental governance,” in which experts, government officials, and everyday people try out different solutions, and make adjustments. Through relentless trial-and-error, implementation creates policy, execution shapes concept, and results accelerate as more of us participate. Does such collaboration seem impossible to you? It shouldn’t. Because AB 32 proved that, even when politics are toxic and the future looks bleak, collaborative governance can change the world. This article was produced by Zócalo .
